title: How Crack Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain crack cocaine: its history from the isolation of cocaine in the mid-1800s through the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914, how freebasing and crack are made, and how crack affects dopamine reuptake in the brain. They cover the health effects, cocaine-alcohol combination (cocaethylene), addiction and withdrawal, and treatment including contingency management. The episode examines the Nicaraguan Contra and CIA drug-link allegations, Gary Webb's Dark Alliance series and the press response to it, and the disparate crack vs. powder cocaine sentencing laws and the 2010 Fair Sentencing Act. It also discusses the crack baby myth, its link to Dr. Ira Chasnoff and the later 25-year study finding poverty, not crack, drove outcomes, and the rise of modern gangs. The episode closes with a listener mail story from Rebecca about a police chase and PTSD.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about 'whack' and the Zach Attack, tease the crack topic, and mention a graffiti artist's message.

segments.title: Cocaine in the 1980s and the crack epidemic
segments.summary: Cocaine was an expensive upscale drug in the 1980s; a cheaper smokable form called crack swept lower-income African American areas, creating an epidemic and drawing Nancy Reagan's concern.

segments.title: Nicaragua, the Contras and CIA drug allegations
segments.summary: Background on the Sandinista revolution and US funding of the Contras. The Kerry/Carry Committee and a CIA internal investigation found Contra-linked drug payments and CIA failure to cut off traffickers, but no proof the CIA deliberately brought drugs in. Hosts note the Nicaraguan Democratic Force was funded partly by cocaine sales sold to Freeway Ricky Ross.

segments.title: Gary Webb and the Dark Alliance series
segments.summary: Gary Webb's San Jose Mercury News series linked the CIA-backed Contra group to Ricky Ross and the crack trade. Major newspapers attacked the series, the Mercury News backed off, and Webb died of a gunshot suicide, which some dispute. A movie about him was mentioned.

segments.title: History of cocaine and the Harrison Act
segments.summary: Cocaine was isolated in the mid-1800s and was widely used and prescribed, including in tonics and by Freud. The Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914 outlawed it, with racially charged justifications.

segments.title: How cocaine, freebase and crack are made
segments.summary: Cocaine powder is made by dissolving coca paste in acid and water and separating it. Freebasing uses ether and is dangerous; Richard Pryor caught fire doing it. Crack is made by boiling cocaine with baking soda or ammonia, hence the name from the crackling sound, and smoked in glass pipes.

segments.title: How crack affects the brain and dopamine
segments.summary: Crack blocks dopamine reuptake through the transporter, leaving dopamine floating in synapses and producing a short, intense high lasting about 5 to 15 minutes. Repeated use can cause the brain to reduce natural dopamine, increasing cravings and withdrawal severity.

segments.title: Health effects, cocaethylene, addiction and treatment
segments.summary: Crack risks heart attack, stroke, and respiratory harm; combined with alcohol it produces cocaethylene, which is toxic to the liver. Withdrawal brings depression and anxiety. No medication specifically treats crack; treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy and contingency management, which rewards abstinence.

segments.title: Street names for crack
segments.summary: Hosts discuss slang for crack such as rock, jelly beans, and French fries, and joke about the made-up-sounding terms.

segments.title: Crack sentencing disparity and the Fair Sentencing Act
segments.summary: Under earlier law, 1 gram of crack drew the same sentence as 100 grams of powder cocaine, and a mandatory five-year minimum applied to crack possession. The Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 changed the ratio to 18 to 1 and removed the mandatory minimum. Eric Holder pushed retroactive releases.

segments.title: The crack baby myth
segments.summary: Dr. Ira Chasnoff's early claims about crack babies spread through the press. A 25-year government study found outcomes tied to poverty and postnatal care rather than crack exposure, and premature babies showed similar symptoms. Alcohol was noted as causing more prenatal harm.

segments.title: Crack and the rise of modern gangs
segments.summary: Hosts say crack's profitability helped create modern inter-city gangs such as the Crips and Bloods, which bought guns and fought over turf.

segments.title: Wrap-up and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts summarize the episode and point listeners to HowStuffWorks for more on crack.

segments.title: Listener mail: police chase and PTSD
segments.summary: Rebecca shares her experience of being hit by teens fleeing police, leading to PTSD and anxiety that she treated with therapy.
